speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what are the Ministry’s plans for Singapore to ease out of Phase Three; (b) what are the specific criteria that must be fulfilled for the current Phase Three restrictions to be lifted; and (c) whether a certain vaccination rate must be achieved before we can explore an exit from Phase Three.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Several weeks ago, we also faced an increase in unlinked cases and community cases in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Hence, even within Phase Three, we had tightened community safe management measures and recalibrated the pace and scale at which activities were able to resume.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While the outbreaks in several countries have abated in recent weeks, we need to remain vigilant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will continue to find ways to allow our economy and our society to further reopen in a safe way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We are also closely monitoring their effectiveness against new viral variants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Singapore has made good progress on our vaccination programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We are continuing to bring in more vaccine supplies, and we encourage all eligible Singaporeans to take up the vaccines to protect themselves and others around them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is reported in the media that if all goes to plan, Singapore will have enough vaccines to vaccinate everyone by the third quarter this year.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We read yesterday that China's Sinovac vaccine arrived in Singapore, but has not been approved for use yet.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will look at the vaccine licensure as an issue of safety and efficacy of a given vaccine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am wondering if he would be willing to share the processes that the Ministry may have in place for if there are outbreaks of more virulent strains of COVID-19 which are not as amenable to the traditional safe management measures, which would render some of our existing procedures less efficacious.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How we apply a given set of safe management measures will very much depend on the burden of disease currently in Singapore and and the risk that our population is exposed to.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This will be a dynamic process as we go forward.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And then, separately, we have to have processes in place to deal with the outbreaks themselves.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the first portion was about how we prevent outbreaks and transmission.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What we will need to calibrate is, for example, how many steps removed you might want to contact trace, how long one quarantines an individual for, and what are the tests before someone is released from a quarantine.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, these are the general processes, but I think when it comes to the specifics of a given viral variant – these are now in a hypothetical space – the key point would be that we take reference from technical and professional advice.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And we are very grateful that we have a depth of technical and professional advice to advise us in fighting COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Integral to safe management and containment is, of course, the process by which we test suspected patients who may be carrying the COVID-19 virus.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister of State, what is the current turnaround time for a PCR swab test?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And the reason I ask this is because one of my residents late last night, contacted me saying on Wednesday morning, he went to the polyclinic and was required to take a swab test.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He has been asked to stay home till the test result comes out and can be confirmed as negative.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, if he does not get the result in time, he may have to cancel the wedding.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, this is a very material question for Singaporeans who may be in a challenging personal situation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, I was wondering if the Senior Minister of State might be able to share a bit more about the timeline for the swab test turnaround.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I do not have the data in front of me.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Parliamentary Question (PQ) was very much about the considerations for Phase Three, Reopening.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would say that the turnaround time is affected by a number of processes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some of them are logistic and administrative as well as the laboratory process itself.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We can follow up with the Member and his constituent separately.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I just want to make an additional point, Mr Speaker, about the question that was raised earlier.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If we do have more vaccines, it is possible that we can accelerate our timeline, but ultimately, this will depend on Singaporeans being willing and coming forward to be vaccinated.
